picks.style: late antique gnomic chant, plainchant over a soft drone, weary male voice, slow, questioning, sparse
picks.why: 'What path of life shall I follow' — every trade and every age indicted in turn, and none of them bearable.

picks.style: riddling incantation, plucked lyre and small bell, low measured voice, unhurried, mounting, mythic
picks.why: The ladder of long lives — crow over man, stag over crow, raven, phoenix, and the nymphs above them all.

picks.style: stoic hymn, bowed strings and held drone, calm grave voice, slow, level, polished
picks.why: The good man as a sphere of the universe, smooth and round, so nothing external can settle on him.

picks.style: greek tragic lament, aulos and frame drum, raw keening female voice, slow, wailing, unresolved
picks.why: Hecuba over Polyxena — 'Achilles even in death still warms his heart with our blood'.

picks.style: epic apparition song, lyre and low drone, warm ghostly male voice, slow, tender, counselling
picks.why: The dead Achilles standing over his son's head to bless and instruct him — an entire farewell in one speech.

picks.style: processional lament, layered female voices over low drone, slow, heavy, tidal
picks.why: The captive Trojan women driven to the ships, and Helen alone not weeping, only burning with shame.

picks.style: roman comic complaint, reed pipe and hand drum, put-upon boyish voice, quick, grumbling, patter
picks.why: The slave boy's solo lament — servitude under a pimp, and a birthday present he cannot pay for.

picks.style: theatrical patter song, tibia and clacking percussion, sly conspiratorial voice, brisk, winking, direct-address
picks.why: Pseudolus turning to the audience: he does not yet know how he will do it, only that it shall be done.

picks.style: comic abuse chorus, double pipe and clappers, trading voices, fast, escalating, gleeful
picks.why: A ladder of insults answered by the pimp agreeing with every one, capped by 'a capital chorus'.

picks.style: scots lament, solo fiddle and small harp, plain unadorned female voice, very slow, bare, grieving
picks.why: 'My waefu' heart lies low wi' his' — a widow's song complete in itself, no ornament anywhere.

picks.style: scots comic strophic song, fiddle and bodhrán, bright sardonic female voice, brisk, dancing, refrain-driven
picks.why: Tibby Fowler rich and pestered — 'but 'cause I'm rich these plaguy men' comes back every stanza.

picks.style: cumbrian dialect ballad, concertina and fiddle, warm old female voice, unhurried, fond, conversational
picks.why: The widow remembering Willy throwing her a daisy over the wall, and 'nea pleace was leyke his awn heame'.

picks.style: methodist hymn, chapel organ and unaccompanied congregation, massed voices, steady, awed, swelling
picks.why: 'Lo God is here! Let us adore' — built for a congregation, with the angel choirs answering the stammering tongue.

picks.style: german pietist hymn, harmonium and low strings, longing solo voice, slow, inward, aching
picks.why: 'I groan, I strive, I watch, I pray: but ah! how soon it dies away' running into 'Thou hidden Love of God'.

picks.style: revival hymn, hand-clapped rhythm and open-air voices, fervent male voice, driving, defiant, rousing
picks.why: 'All hail, Reproach, and welcome Pain!' — the missionary's whole nerve in four lines.

picks.style: english winter air, guitar and recorder, gentle tenor, unhurried, hearth-warm, small
picks.why: The robin hopping over the threshold to peck crumbs, the one singer left when the rest have gone silent.

picks.style: passing-bell elegy, tolling bell and low strings, solemn baritone, slow, arresting, spacious
picks.why: 'Hark! — what a mournful solemn sound' — the bell itself is the refrain and the whole occasion.

picks.style: graveside air, viola and harp, clear soprano, slow, tender, valedictory
picks.why: 'Like those she bloom'd, and ah! like these she fell' — roses and lilies made to say the whole epitaph.

picks.style: roman prophetic dirge, low strings and struck bronze, grave male voice, slow, fated, hollow
picks.why: Only candidate, but it carries the Marcellus lines the old emperor sang over his own son — shown to the earth and no longer.
